Joshua. The military leader and judge who succeeded Moses and led the Israelites into the Promised Land of Canaan after forty years of wilderness wandering. Where Moses was the lawgiver and liberator from Egypt, Joshua became the conqueror and consolidator—his campaigns against the Canaanite kingdoms are narrated in the book bearing his name, and he represents the transition from nomadic desert life to settled agricultural existence. His strategic brilliance and faith in God's guidance made him the paradigmatic warrior-leader of the Hebrew Bible.

Joshua was originally named Hosea but Moses renamed him Joshua, meaning the Lord saves, signaling his destined role in leading Israel to salvation in the promised land. He was one of twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan, and only he and Caleb returned with faith that Israel could conquer the land, though he was forced to wait forty years as punishment for the people's doubt. After Moses's death, God appointed Joshua as the new leader of Israel, and the book of Joshua narrates his military campaigns to conquer the land west of the Jordan River.

The miraculous crossing of the Jordan River on dry ground paralleled the crossing of the Red Sea under Moses, establishing Joshua's legitimacy as Moses's successor. The most famous episode is the siege of Jericho, where the Israelite army marched around the city walls for seven days, and on the seventh day, they trumpeted and the walls collapsed, allowing entry. Joshua divided the conquered territory among the twelve tribes of Israel, establishing tribal borders and inheritance portions that became foundational to Israelite settlement patterns. At the end of his life, Joshua gathered the Israelites and led a covenant renewal ceremony, reaffirming their commitment to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
